theme: Give thanks to the LORD; remember his covenant
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 105:1-15. You read this in earlier units as a recital of God’s covenant faithfulness. The first fifteen verses were also part of David’s song in 1 Chronicles 16. Notice how the song uses the covenant with Abraham as a ground for present thanks.
settingTheScene: Psalm 105 is a long historical psalm, recounting God’s care of Israel from Abraham to the conquest. The first fifteen verses were sung on the day the ark came to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:8-22). They set out the call to remember and then the heart of what they were to remember: the covenant. The returned exiles were reading this in a time when the land was again precarious. It reminded them that the promise to Abraham did not depend on their strength.
observation: “Oh give thanks to the LORD; call upon his name; make known his deeds among the peoples!” (v. 1).
“Sing to him, sing praises to him; tell of all his wondrous works!” (v. 2).
“Let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice!” (v. 3).
“Seek the LORD and his strength; seek his presence continually!” (v. 4).
“Remember the wondrous works that he has done, his miracles, and the judgments he uttered” (v. 5).
“He is the LORD our God; his judgments are in all the earth” (v. 7).
“He remembers his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations” (v. 8).
“When they were few in number, of little account, and sojourners in it” (v. 12).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with a string of imperatives, nine in a row: give thanks, call, make known, sing, sing praises, tell, glory, rejoice, seek. Worship in Scripture is active, public, and full of verbs. Notice verse 3: “Let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice.” Seeking, which is often hard, is joyful.

Verse 5 gives the central command: remember. “Remember the wondrous works that he has done.” The main work of faith is memory. We forget so easily. The returned exiles had been through trauma, and remembering God’s past acts was how they kept hope alive. For you too, remembering is a spiritual discipline. Keep a journal, mark anniversaries, tell stories.

The heart of the psalm is verses 8 to 11: God “remembers his covenant forever.” Not just for one or two generations, but “for a thousand generations.” The covenant given to Abraham, repeated to Isaac and Jacob, includes the promise of Canaan. That promise was kept even though Israel was “few in number, of little account, and sojourners.” The people were small, weak, and wandering, yet God protected them: “He allowed no one to oppress them; he rebuked kings on their account.” Pharaoh and Abimelech are the examples. God said of the patriarchs, “Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm.”

For the post-exilic community, the phrase “few in number, of little account” described them exactly. And the psalm tells them that their smallness did not matter to God. The covenant he made held them. This is a major part of the Chronicler’s message: you are small, but you are the people to whom God made promises, and he will keep them.
connection: Luke 22:19: “Do this in remembrance of me.” Deuteronomy 7:7-9 says God did not set his love on Israel because they were many, but because he loved them and kept his oath. 1 Corinthians 1:26-29 says God chooses the weak and lowly. Galatians 3:29: “If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring.” Luke 1:72-73 says God remembered his holy covenant. Matthew 28:20: “I am with you always.”
application:
Make a list of ten “wondrous works” of God in your life. Read it aloud this week.

Take the Lord’s Supper, or think about it if you are not able, and remember Christ’s work.

Seek the LORD’s presence continually: set a time each day to be still with him.
prayerPrompts: Give thanks and remember his wondrous works, naming one.
Thank him that he remembers his covenant forever.
Ask him to let you seek his face always.
